articles.title: Hawaii’s famed Hōlei Sea Arch has collapsed
articles.summary: A colossal sea arch that had long been a major landmark on Hawaii’s rugged coastline has collapsed into the Pacific Ocean more than 500 years after it was naturally formed, the local park service confirmed.
articles.body: A colossal sea arch that had long been a major landmark on Hawaii’s rugged coastline has collapsed into the Pacific Ocean more than 500 years after it was naturally formed, the local park service confirmed. Hōlei Sea Arch stood at a height of roughly 90 feet (27 meters) in Hawaii’s Volcanoes National Park on the southern coast of the Big Island — the largest and youngest island of the Hawaiian chain. The arch formed around 550 years ago when ancient lava flow from the eruption of one of the island’s six volcanoes hit the cliff edges and carved the vault, creating a natural marvel that drew visitors to the spot for many years, according to the United States National Park Service (NPS). While the exact time of the collapse is unknown, the Volcanoes National Park team said on social media Thursday that the arch was still standing on Wednesday, September 23, when the park was temporarily closed during Tropical Storm Nolo. When it reopened on Monday, 28 September, the arch was gone. “Yes, it’s true. RIP Hōlei Sea Arch,” Volcanoes National Park said in posts of Facebook and Instagram, alongside before-and-after photographs revealing a stark shift in the scenery. “Hōlei Sea Arch was a very special place to so many of our visitors,” it added. But the wild and remote coastline’s dramatic transformation had long been expected, according to NPS. “This formation is beautiful, but temporary, and has a limited life span,” NPS said in a description of the beauty spot on its website. “The sea arch will eventually crumble into the sea. However, others will replace it as the cliff slowly migrates inland,” it added. NPS said the cliff’s lifespan was determined by differential erosion — a process whereby softer rock is worn away faster and harder than stronger, more resistant rock. Landscapes are routinely reshaped through differential erosion, and it is how the arch came to be more than five centuries ago. Park staff knew the incessant battering of waves against the sea arch would eventually cause it to crumble into the Pacific, although they were not able to predict exactly when this would happen. Volcanoes National Park urged visitors to keep their distance from the unstable cliff edges to avoid putting themselves, or first responders, in danger.

images.caption: Hawaii's famed Holei Sea Arch has collapsed due to differential erosion.
An image from September 30 shows empty space where the Hōlei Sea Arch used to be.
The Hōlei Sea Arch was formed roughly 550 years ago.

articles.title: Dolly Parton sings Jolene in Welsh in recording released after her death
articles.summary: Parton's niece Jada Star and Welsh singer Bronwen Lewis say the country artist was proud to sing in Welsh.
articles.body:
A new version of Dolly Parton's Jolene is set to be released, with parts of the song sung in Welsh by the legendary country artist.

The song was recorded before her death on 25 August , and is a collaboration with Welsh singer-songwriter Bronwen Lewis as well as Parton's niece, Jada Star.

In a seven-decade career, Parton won 10 Grammy awards, sold more than 100 million records worldwide, and wrote more than 3,000 songs.

The single will come out on 9 October, and is the second posthumous release from Parton - who was of Welsh descent.

In a teaser video released on social media, Star and Lewis explained how the song came to light.

As a proud Welsh speaker, Lewis, from Neath, had started translating some of her favourite tunes, and soon landed on the Parton classic, Jolene.

"Two years ago I posted a video of me singing the Dolly Parton classic Jolene in Welsh ," said Lewis.

"I never expected it would go viral and definitely didn't expect it to attract the attention of Dolly's family - especially her niece Jada."

A friendship was born, and Star came over from Nashville in the US to Wales to meet Lewis, joining her at Pride Cymru.

"Pride Cymru was such an amazing experience and I learned so much about my family lineage," said Star.

"I cherish the time I spent with Bronwen exploring one of the most beautiful places I have ever seen."

The teaser revealed it was Star's suggestion to record Jolene in Welsh, which Lewis "jumped" at the chance to do, with Star then saying she would get her aunt involved too.

"Jada told me that her Aunt Dolly would like to sing with us on our version of Jolene. I think I fell to the ground," said Lewis.

"Definitely cried happy tears, and called my mother immediately."

BBC Radio Wales presenter Lewis said she had always loved Parton's music.

"To hear Dolly sing in another language, and in Welsh for the very first time, was unbelievable."

After understanding the phonetics of Lewis' translation, Parton recorded her parts at her studio in Nashville, in early 2025.

Lewis had planned to go over to meet her to release the music, but Parton passed away before the meet-up could happen.

"It was devastating, not just for myself and our family, but for the entire world," Star said.

Lewis said the pair realised what a privilege it was to have recorded and collaborated "with one of the greatest musicians and women to grace this Earth".

"We did what she always told us to do. We got ourselves together and decided to finish what we started," Star added.

Star and Lewis said Parton was "proud" to sing in Welsh.

This is not the first time Parton has featured on songs in another language.

She has appeared on several Latin songs and also collaborated on a track with an Irish folk band in 2011.

Before her death, Parton revealed she had recorded a song with U2 which is set to be released in November. She also teased fans about a track which has been kept in a time capsule until its planned release in 2046.

In 2008, during a concert at the Cardiff International Arena, Parton reportedly revealed her Welsh ancestry to fans in the crowd.

"Some of my mother's people, the Owens, are from there [Wales]," Parton later told Wales Online.

"I've been there about three times and it always feels good because it feels like family."

Star had also previously spoken about the family's Welsh connection.

She said the Owens side of the family, coming from Parton's mother Avie Lee Owens, was believed to have come from Conwy.

Speaking to BBC Radio Wales in 2024, Star said discovering that part of the family's history had been "really extraordinary".

Star suggested some of Parton's music, and her own, may have been inspired by her Welsh roots.

Parton's death brought renewed attention in Wales to the country music legend's Welsh links, with her heritage explored in a 2025 documentary.

Following the singer's death, research by staff at Conwy council's archives suggested Parton's ancestors were from Machynlleth, not Conwy as previously thought.

articles.title: G7 to release 100m oil barrels as Trump hails Europe diesel deal
articles.summary: Macron says G7 will release 100 million barrels over four months; diesel release to be ‘frontloaded’.
articles.body:
Members of the Group of Seven (G7) have announced they will release up to 100 million barrels of strategic oil reserves as prices continue to soar amid the United States-Israeli war with Iran.

In a statement following a meeting chaired by French President Emmanuel Macron, the group said the release would be coordinated through the International Energy Agency (IEA) over the next four months. It added the release will include “a frontloaded substantial diesel release within the first 20 days by G7 members and partners”.

The group said it will “convene in the context of the IEA in the coming days to discuss the possibility of additional diesel releases as necessary”.

The announcement came just moments after US President Donald Trump said in a post on his Truth Social account that Europe had “just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil”.

The G7, composed of the world’s top economies, includes Canada and the US as well as several European powers, including France, Germany, Italy and the United Kingdom. The European Union is also an observer member of the grouping.

Trump has recently pressured European countries, notably Germany and France, to release diesel stockpiles to ease soaring prices caused by constrictions on shipping traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, which many European officials have met with wariness.

High global energy prices have been a knock-on effect of the war with Iran, which Trump launched alongside Israel on February 28.

According to Eurostat’s June 2026 data, EU countries, along with the United Kingdom, hold about 52 million tonnes of gas, oil and diesel stocks. That includes nearly 38 million tonnes of emergency reserves held by EU countries.

EU rules require member states to maintain emergency oil stocks covering at least 90 days of net imports or 61 days of domestic consumption, whichever is greater.

Trump had previously floated banning US diesel exports if European countries did not release their stockpiles.

The EU, composed of several members that rely heavily on diesel imports, said earlier on Friday that it fully rejected that threat.

The national average for a gallon of diesel in the US was $6.37 on Friday, according to the American Automobile Association. The average hit a record high of $6.52 on September 22.

The issue has been politically damaging for Trump and his Republican Party ahead of the US midterm elections in November, with Trump’s approval on the economy plunging as the vote approaches.

Diesel is fundamental to many top US industries, including transportation, construction and agriculture.

US diesel inventories hit a record low of 107.9 million barrels as of September 11, 2026.

In March, the IEA’s 32 member countries agreed to unlock 400 million barrels of oil from their emergency reserves. Officials have said that the release has not yet been fully completed.

articles.title: France’s teen riots take explosive new turn as government points finger at hard left
articles.summary: Riot police clashed with teenagers across France as roughly 400 high schools closed and some 2,000 people were arrested amid escalating student unrest.
articles.body: Violent student unrest intensified across France on Friday as riot police clashed with teenagers in several cities, roughly 400 high schools remained shuttered and authorities said some 2,000 people had been arrested since the protests began — while the government increasingly blamed the country’s hard left. Tear gas filled streets in Strasbourg, protesters fired fireworks toward police lines in Marseille, and garbage bins were set ablaze in Rennes, while clashes also broke out in Paris, Reuters reported Friday. The latest violence marks a sharp escalation from the unrestt reported by Fox News Digital Thursday, when hundreds had been arrested as school blockades and clashes spread across the country. Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin told RTL radio Friday that approximately 2,000 people — most of them teenagers — had been arrested since the protests erupted. He said parents whose children damage property should be required to pay reparations, according to Reuters. "In the streets, the children are in danger," Education Minister Édouard Geffray told BFM TV. ISRAELI AMBASSADOR COMPARES FRANCE'S FAR-LEFT LEADER'S RHETORIC TO HITLER AS ANTISEMITISM SURGES Euronews reported Friday that at least 65 school staff members, including 40 principals, have been injured since the unrest began, along with roughly 170 students. More than 100 high schools have suffered what Geffray described as "severe damage." The protests began over complaints about overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages, long school days and deteriorating facilities. Students have blamed years of underinvestment for conditions inside schools, as the government unveiled its draft 2027 budget Thursday. Under the proposal, education spending would rise 1.7% to 65.53 billion euros, excluding teacher pensions — an increase below the rate of inflation, according to Reuters. But as the protests have grown more violent, the unrest has also become a major political fight. French intelligence agencies told a government crisis meeting Thursday that the protest movement had been initiated by politicians from the hard-left France Unbowed Party, known as LFI, Reuters reported Friday. FRENCH COURT CLEARS PATH FOR CONSERVATIVE PRESIDENTIAL CANDIDATE, BUT HOUSE ARREST THREATENS CAMPAIGN LFI lawmakers rejected the allegation and accused President Emmanuel Macron's government of politicizing the protests ahead of France's 2027 presidential election. Le Monde reported Friday that Geffray accused LFI of fueling the initial demonstrations before saying the movement had been "taken hostage by ultra-left groups." LFI leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon has denied responsibility for the violence. Simone Rodan-Benzaquen, senior envoy to Europe at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, told Fox News Digital on Thursday that the unrest began with legitimate concerns but has since evolved into something far more serious. "The students’ grievances about missing teachers and deteriorating schools were real at first," Rodan-Benzaquen said. "But dousing a principal in gasoline and attacking firefighters are acts of extreme violence. What makes this politically significant is the effort to turn frustration over schools into a much broader confrontation with the government." The protests are quickly becoming a major issue in the campaign to succeed Macron next May, with Mélenchon denouncing the government’s response as repressive. Rodan-Benzaquen said LFI has "actively supported the mobilization," adding that "activists circulate footage of clashes, party accounts amplify it and elected officials present themselves as the students’ defenders." "With an election next year," she said, "Mélenchon sees these mobilizations as a way to consolidate young voters and marginalize the moderate left. At a time of deep political, geopolitical and economic challenges, this is a very dangerous situation for France." Marine Le Pen also accused LFI of playing a direct role in the unrest. "This is no longer about high school student protests. It is about riots organized by professionals and overseen by deputies from La France Insoumise," Le Pen wrote on X in a translated post. "We must pass a new anti-rioters law so that participation in a riot is a clearly identified offense." PSG CHAMPIONS LEAGUE VICTORY CAUSES CHAOS IN PARIS, WITH 45 ARRESTED AND FIRES SET ACROSS CITY The government has now deployed specialized riot police and mobile gendarmes as authorities struggle to contain the unrest, Le Monde reported. The government's response is also drawing scrutiny. Students and rights groups have accused police of excessive force against minors, including the use of batons, tear gas and non-lethal weapons. Amnesty International warned against excessive force, while France's Interior Ministry said Friday that three investigations into alleged police violence had been opened, according to Reuters. The unrest may also be beginning to spread beyond France. Students in Liège, Belgium, began demonstrating Thursday, and high schools there were closed Friday. articles.title: Greens can move Labour in the right direction, says Zack Polanski
articles.summary: The Green leader tells his autumn conference that a vote for his party can force changes from Andy Burnham.
articles.body:
Zack Polanski has urged voters to back the Greens to force changes from Andy Burnham, arguing his party has the power to move Labour in "the right direction".

In his speech to the party's annual conference, the Green leader said that "sustained pressure" from his party had made forced Labour into changing its stance on issues including climate and its stance towards Israel.

He told activists in Brighton that Labour had failed to take action on housing, as he called for a three-year cap to limit rent rises in the private sector.

And he said that voting for the Greens would force changes from the government, telling members: "Vote Green, and watch Labour move".

Polanski arrived in Brighton facing questions over his leadership of the party amid signs the Greens' rise in popularity last year may have waned, and how he would respond to Labour's change of leadership under Burnham.

In his half-hour address, he did not mention the Conservatives or Reform UK but launched repeated attacks on Labour's record in office.

He criticised Labour for making "slogans without action" on the cost of living and vowed only his party would end "Rip Off Britain".

And he was particularly critical of Labour's record on housing, where he accused the party of failing to take on the "powerful vested interests of developers and big landlords".

Instead, he urged the government to enact an "emergency brake" on private rents, under which they would be prevented from rising above the lowest of consumer price index measure of inflation, wage growth or 2%, for three years.

He argued that pressure from the Greens in the face of government "inaction" had forced Burnham into calling an emergency Cobr meeting this summer amid record-breaking hot and dry temperatures.

The Greens, he added would not "hesitate" to tax "extreme wealth", as he repeated the party's call for a so-called windfall tax on back profits - an issue where the government has faced pressure from unions.

"Through our sustained pressure – and our historic wins – we have held the worst instincts of the Labour government in check.

"And we have started to move them in the right direction. But we can't wait for them to get there on their own."

He also sought to draw a clear dividing line with the government on the issue of oil and gas, ahead of looming decisions for the government on whether to approve the Rosebank oil field and Jackdaw gas field.

Burnham has stuck to Labour's manifesto commitment not to issue new oil and gas licences, but has left open the possibility of approving the two sites.

This summer's wildfires, Polanski told the conference hall, should prove the "final nail in the coffin for new oil and gas".

He began his address by celebrating his party's surge in membership since his election as party leader a year ago, and electoral successes including the hundreds of councillors it gained in May's local elections in England .

But his speech did not touch on an issue that could divide the membership over the weekend, ahead of a probable vote on a motion put forward by members that describes Zionism as a form of racism.

The motion defines Zionism as an ideology in support of "an ethnonationalist Jewish state" and seeks to shift the party's position to supporting a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine".

The current form of the motion has drawn criticism from senior figures, including deputy leader Rachel Millward, who earlier described it as "problematic".

Before the conference, Polanski declined to say whether he would support the motion in its current form but said he wanted to see it changed.

He has said he wants to see the motion amended to specify that it should not be used to discipline Jewish members attending synagogues that consider themselves Zionist.

He is also supporting a change that would replace the call for a single Palestinian state with backing for a "lasting settlement granting equal rights for all" to be "shaped and determined by Palestinians themselves".

articles.title: A Delaware school got $1 million from an anonymous donor when it opened; one year later, the donor returned with $2 million
articles.summary: When Holy Cross High School opened its doors in Delaware in 2025, an anonymous donor gave the new school $1 million to help it through its first year.
articles.body: When Holy Cross High School opened its doors in Delaware in 2025, an anonymous donor gave the new school $1 million to help it through its first year. One year later, on the first day of the school's second academic year, the same donor contacted Head of School Tom Fertal again with another unexpected gift, this time worth $2 million. The donor has asked to remain anonymous, while the school refers to the person as its “Angel Investor”. The latest contribution comes as Holy Cross works to establish a permanent campus in Frederica, where it has secured about 100 acres of land. The school is now developing plans for a new campus that it hopes to open in 2028.The first $1 million came when the school openedHoly Cross High School began operating in autumn 2025 as an independent Catholic high school serving families in Kent and Sussex counties. It was established to provide a Catholic high-school option in an area that had been without one since the closure of St Thomas More Academy in 2020.The school initially operated from a temporary location in Dover while working towards its long-term campus. From the outset, school leaders envisioned moving into a dedicated facility as enrolment and programmes expanded.That plan received an early boost on the very day Holy Cross opened.The anonymous donor contacted Fertal and gave the school $1 million to support its inaugural year. The contribution arrived as the new institution was beginning to establish its academic programmes, build enrolment and develop the financial foundation needed for future growth.At the time, the donor's identity was not disclosed, and the school has continued to keep it private.Then the same donor came back with $2 millionThe next contribution arrived with remarkably similar timing.According to The Dialog, Fertal was contacted by the same donor on the first day of the 2026-27 school year, exactly as Holy Cross began its second academic year. Instead of another introductory gift, the donor committed $2 million.The school refers to the anonymous benefactor as its “Angel Investor”. With the latest contribution, the donor has now given Holy Cross a total of $3 million across its first two years.The timing of the gifts has made the donor's support an unusual part of the school's short history. The first donation came as Holy Cross opened its doors for the first time, while the second arrived as students and staff returned for year two.Brian Lessard, chair of the school's board of trustees, said the donor's backing had also helped encourage others to support the school's broader fundraising effort.The money comes as Holy Cross prepares to buildThe $2 million gift arrives at a pivotal stage for Holy Cross.The school has secured about 100 acres in Frederica, Delaware, where it plans to develop its permanent campus. Its Founders Campaign is focused on turning the property into a long-term home for the school and its growing programmes.The proposed campus would be a major expansion from the temporary facilities where Holy Cross began.Plans call for a main school building of roughly 90,600 square feet, along with facilities including a chapel, technology centre, medical sciences suite, theatre, art and music spaces, gymnasium and broadcast studio. The wider development is also planned to include athletic fields, tennis courts and additional buildings.Construction is expected to begin around 2027, with the school targeting an autumn 2028 opening for the permanent campus, subject to the development process.A school that started with about 35 studentsHoly Cross' ambitions are considerably larger than its first-year footprint.Before opening in 2025, the school expected around 35 students for its inaugural year. Most were expected to be freshmen, with a smaller number entering as sophomores. The school planned to add higher grades as those initial cohorts progressed.That gradual expansion was part of the reason a permanent campus became central to the school's plans. A dedicated facility would provide room for the academic, extracurricular, athletic and spiritual programmes envisioned by school leaders.Holy Cross operates independently rather than as a school directly funded by the Diocese of Wilmington. Its finances therefore depend on sources including tuition, private donations and fundraising.The $2 million gift supports the next stageThe latest donation gives the school's permanent-campus campaign another major contribution as Holy Cross moves from its first years of operation towards a larger, purpose-built institution.The school is now working towards developing its 100-acre Frederica property into a campus capable of supporting the students it expects to serve in the years ahead.For an institution that only opened in 2025, the two donations have provided an unusual beginning: $1 million when the school opened, followed by another $2 million when its second academic year began.The donor's identity remains private, but the two gifts have already made the anonymous benefactor one of the most significant supporters in Holy Cross High School's early history.You use AI every day. articles.title: Former priest Chris Brain guilty of raping and assaulting women
articles.summary: The leader of Sheffield's former Nine O'Clock Service movement is facing prison for abusing 13 women.
articles.body:
A former priest who established a "cult" within the Church of England has been found guilty of raping a woman in his congregation.

Chris Brain was also convicted of four counts of indecent assault against three other women who were part of the Nine O'Clock Service in Sheffield in the 1980s and 1990s.

The 69-year-old was found guilty of the offences after a retrial at Inner London Crown Court, having already been found guilty of 17 indecent assaults against nine women at a trial last year.

Brain, previously of Wilmslow in Greater Manchester, is in custody awaiting sentencing at a later date.

The Nine O'Clock Service, known as NOS, attracted hundreds of young people to St Thomas's church with its ground-breaking nightclub-style worship which blended rave culture, live music and prayer.

But jurors heard the group "became a cult" in which members were encouraged to cut themselves off from family and friends, leaving them "utterly dependent" on Brain, and living in fear of being ostracised if they crossed him.

Prosecutor Tim Clark KC told the court Brain had abused his position as a priest to sexually assault "a staggering number of women from his congregation".

The verdicts mean Brain has now been convicted of a total of 22 sexual offences against 13 women.

Following his latest convictions, South Yorkshire Police said Brain was a "devious and arrogant sexual predator who caused lasting harm to these women".

Across the two trials the court heard several of Brain's victims were part of a so-called "homebase team", who cared for him 24 hours a day in his family home and would be expected to "put him to bed" with sexual massages.

One woman told the court how Brain had pushed her down onto his bed and raped her after inviting her to his house while his wife was away between 1981 and 1984.

Another victim said in evidence at both trials she was sexually assaulted by the priest in her bedroom while traumatised after spending hours helping people at the Hillsborough disaster locate the bodies of friends and family.

Brain, who quit as a priest when allegations about his conduct were first publicly raised in 1995, accepted having sexual contact with some of the women but told the court it had always been consensual.

In an Everyman Special documentary broadcast by BBC One in November 1995, Brain admitted sexual activity with women members of NOS but denied it was abuse and said it was for "closeness and affection", the court heard.

In a statement released after Friday's verdicts, one of Brain's victims from the first trial said she and the other women had waited more than 30 years for justice, adding the delay should be a "cause of great shame for the Church of England".

She said church leaders had "ignored warning signs" about Brain and "utterly failed in their duty of care".

"Our continued healing is not dependent on this guilty verdict," the woman said.

"But at last the immense pain this man inflicted has been acknowledged, he is finally accountable and we can continue to move forward."

She added: "This group of women are without doubt the best, bravest and smartest women you could ever know and I am so very proud of us all."

Brain's trials heard at least two members of clergy had raised concerns about him with the Diocese of Sheffield years before he was stopped.

After Brain was first convicted in August 2025 , the Bishop of Sheffield, the Rt Rev Dr Pete Wilcox, apologised for "institutional failures" and announced an independent safeguarding into its response.

In a statement following the latest verdicts on Friday, he said: "My first thoughts today are with the women whose courage brought this retrial to a conclusion. They have now given evidence, in full, not once but twice.

"I am acutely conscious of the cost it has had for them.

"Last year I offered an unreserved apology for the abuse of power and leadership that took place within the Nine O'Clock Service. Today's verdict adds to that same picture, and my apology stands in full."

Lawyer Richard Scorer, who is representing the women in civil action against the Church of England, called Brain a "serial abuser".

"But we mustn't forget that he was fast-tracked to ordination, supported, promoted and protected by the Church of England," he added.

"A full accounting of their role in this appalling saga is long overdue and must now follow."

Julie Moss, senior crown prosecutor for Yorkshire and Humberside, said Brain had perpetrated "a disturbing campaign of manipulation and abuse".

She added: "Victims were isolated from their loved ones, made financially and emotionally dependent on the group, and made to believe that resistance to Brain's sexual advances reflected their own personal or spiritual failings."

Det Supt Eleanor Welsh, of South Yorkshire Police, said: "These women have waited three or four decades for these verdicts and bravely relived their ordeals in a bid to secure justice."

Judge Freya Newbury said victims would be given the chance to deliver impact statements at a sentencing hearing, which is likely to take two days.

articles.summary: New York Governor Kathy Hochul has removed Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten from overseeing the investigation into an alleged gang
articles.body: New York Governor Kathy Hochul has removed Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten from overseeing the investigation into an alleged gang rape at Cornell University and handed the case to state Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor.Hochul signed an executive order appointing James to take over the investigation after saying she had lost faith in Van Houten's ability to fairly handle the case. The move came after newly released information raised questions about how Cornell police and the district attorney's office handled the allegations, according to the Associated Press.The case involves a former Cornell student identified as Jane Doe, who has alleged that she was drugged with ketamine and sexually assaulted by seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity at the university's Ithaca campus in October 2024. articles.title: Intensified Russian strikes are tearing Kyiv apart, Klitschko warns
articles.summary: Vitaliy Klitschko says Ukraine's capital is in a "very dramatic situation" as Russia hits critical infrastructure.
articles.body:
Intensified Russian drone and missile strikes are "tearing Kyiv apart", the mayor of Ukraine's capital has warned.

Vitaliy Klitschko said the city was now in a "very dramatic situation" as Moscow was battering its "critical infrastructure, logistics, housing" and other key facilities.

He was speaking after Kyiv's defence council held a crisis meeting, following new Russian strikes on a key bridge that caused traffic chaos. The city's data centres have also been recently hit, resulting in internet outages.

President Vladimir Putin earlier said Russia was acting in response to Ukraine's strikes on Russian energy facilities, despite the fact that it was Moscow that had first launched such attacks.

"We're talking about survival," Klitschko said at Friday's defence council meeting with Kyiv's top military, security, emergencies and police officials.

Russia's aim was to "sow panic", he said, stressing that the capital would "prevail - but only through the joint efforts of those who love it and care for it".

The mayor was speaking just hours after Kyiv's key Pivdennyi (Southern) bridge was hit in an overnight Russian drone attack. On Friday evening it was struck again - the fourth time in two days.

The bridge is one of the main transport arteries across the Dnipro River dividing western and eastern parts of Kyiv.

All metro and automobile traffic is now suspended across the bridge, causing major delays across the city. Restrictions are also in place on Kyiv's two other key bridges.

Kyiv's current population is estimated to be about three million, and many residents rely heavily on the city's metro network.

One person was killed in the capital when a multi-storey residential building was hit overnight, Ukraine's state emergencies service DSNS said.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Putin had decided in early September that "there are no rules now" when attacking Ukraine.

In a published excerpt from his interview with the Financial Times, Zelensky said: "The Russians have failed to occupy us. So now they are carrying out massive attacks and mass killings.

"They want to destroy our bridges... our data centres, the internet, mobile networks, hospitals, kindergartens, schools, universities - everything. They want people to flee their cities."

Putin insisted that Russia's attacks on Ukrainian economic targets were a direct response to Ukraine's strikes on Russia's oil refineries and its ships in the Black Sea.

"Now from every direction we're receiving calls 'let's stop'. But they started it," Putin said after a wide-ranging speech at the Valdai foreign policy forum on Thursday.

Putin admitted Kyiv had "got some results" from its refinery attacks and Russia had lost about 1% of its GDP. Ukraine maintains it began attacking Russian oil infrastructure because it helps the Kremlin finance the war.

Russia has targeted Ukrainian energy infrastructure, ramping up attacks every winter since Putin launched a full-scale invasion in 2022.

articles.title: Ukraine says it forced 250 Russian soldiers to surrender in daring operation
articles.summary: A daredevil Ukrainian operation using robots dropped behind enemy lines and “Trojan” armored personnel carriers laden with explosives has led to the capture of more than 250 Russian troops, Kyiv has announced.
articles.body: A daredevil Ukrainian operation using robots dropped behind enemy lines and “Trojan” armored personnel carriers laden with explosives has led to the capture of more than 250 Russian troops, Kyiv says. Ukraine’s army has been chipping away at Russian-controlled territories in the eastern Ukrainian region of Donbas as part of a counteroffensive operation dubbed “Vivaldi.” Its successes have provided a spark of optimism in what has otherwise been a bleak few months for Ukraine. A video of the surrendering Russians, shared by Ukraine’s Third Army Corps this week, shows dozens of men walking through a forest in single file, forming a long human chain. Heads down, they are closely guarded by their Ukrainian captors who then herd them into a tight formation and make them conduct an improvised rollcall. The video shows some of the Russian prisoners explaining that they surrendered because they “didn’t want to die in vain” and describing eating bark and grass as well as drinking from puddles after running out of the most basic provisions. CNN cannot independently verify the video or Ukrainian claims about the surrender, but some prominent Russian military bloggers have lamented recent Ukrainian advances and demanded answers from the Russian leadership over the reports of command failures and supply shortages that led to the surrenders. Russia has been pummeling Ukrainian cities with near non-stop aerial attacks, taking advantage of Kyiv’s critical shortages of air defense missiles. The past four months have been among the deadliest for Ukrainian civilians since the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022. Operation Vivaldi has been largely defined by Ukraine’s innovative use of technology, especially aerial and ground drones and armored personal carriers. During one assault operation, Ukrainian military managed to airdrop robotic systems equipped with heavy guns more than 10 kilometers (6.2 miles) behind the Russian lines, according to Andriy Biletskyi, the commander of the Third Army Corps . Controlled from the safety of command centers deep inside Ukraine-held territory, these land drones were then able to attack Russian troops from an unexpected direction. The skies above the front lines in Ukraine have been swarming with drones for years now, posing a threat to infantry so grave it has forced Ukraine to make ground robots an integral part of its arsenal. These land drones are much harder to spot and intercept than larger military vehicles. Compared with their aerial counterparts, they can operate in all weather conditions and carry much larger payloads. But Operation Vivaldi is the first time they are known to have been smuggled behind Russia’s defensive lines. In another innovation, the Third Army Corps converted old Soviet-era armored personnel carriers into unmanned kamikaze ground vehicles by stuffing them with explosives and sending them towards Russian fortification, prompting Ukraine’s military to refer to them as “Trojan” tanks. After three months of small but steady Russian gains, the situation flipped in September when Russia lost more Ukrainian territory than it seized. Experts at the Institute for the Study of War (ISW), a US-based conflict monitor, calculated that while Russian forces seized about 175 square kilometers (67 square miles) in September, they elsewhere lost 256 square kilometers (99 square miles). Operation Vivaldi played a key role in this – allowing Ukraine to recapture nearly 150 square kilometers (58 square miles), according to the ISW. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky put the gains made by Vivaldi even higher, saying 176 square kilometers (68 square miles) had been recaptured and 5,000 Russian troops either wounded or killed since the operation started. The losses have been noticed in Russia – Rybar, one of the most prominent pro-Kremlin Russian military bloggers, has taken to Telegram to complain about the “deteriorating” situation, saying Russian troops will now be “forced to reorganize their logistics and adjust the pace of their advance on both Slovyansk and Kramatorsk.” Russian President Vladimir Putin desperately wants to seize Ukraine’s eastern Donbas region, and the two cities which form a part of Ukraine’s defenses are a key obstacle in that goal. Speaking at the Valdai Club, a Moscow-based discussion forum, on Thursday, Putin claimed that Europe and Ukraine fear Kyiv can withstand Russia’s advances for only another 18-24 months. Putin suggested Moscow could take the remainder of Donetsk in even less time and Ukrainian resistance was futile However, the Vivaldi Operation has raised hopes in Kyiv that Russia may not be capable of taking the rest of the Donbas so quickly. While Moscow has been slowly chipping away at the so-called “fortress belt” in the east, its advances have been slow and costly. Western intelligence services estimate Russia is losing some 40,000 troops a month – a rate of roughly 340 casualties for every square kilometer. The ISW has calculated that at their current pace, Russian forces would not take over the rest of the Donbas until 2032 — if they can seize it at all.

articles.title: Alison Hammond has heart check-up in hospital after rushing off This Morning while on air
articles.summary: The host says she is "fine" but getting checked after leaving midway through Friday's This Morning.
articles.body:
Alison Hammond went to hospital for a heart check-up after leaving ITV's This Morning midway through Friday's show, but has assured followers she is "fine".

The presenter, 51, left the programme during its live broadcast, appearing to clutch her chest as she was assisted off the set by co-host Dermot O'Leary. He later told viewers she was "feeling a little unwell".

In a video posted from a hospital bed on Friday afternoon, Hammond said she had "a little bit of a palpitation" during the show but was feeling OK and was undergoing tests.

"I know you're all worried about me," she said. "Honestly, I am fine. First of all, I'm getting my old ticker checked out."

She continued: "I had a little bit of a palpitation, and now I'm getting it all checked out. But I think I'm OK. I'm hoping it was just a little panic attack or something like that."

The Birmingham-born presenter, who also co-hosts The Great British Bake Off, thanked This Morning's viewers for sending her "lovely messages" while apologising for her dramatic early exit.

"I'm so sorry I left you," she added. "I would never normally do that. I would never leave a TV show, so you know I wasn't very well.

"But hopefully I'm going to be all right. The doctors are so lovely, and they're checking me out, and hopefully everything's going to be fine.

"Everything is fine, look. I'm rocking it. Look how good I look," she joked, noting how she was still wearing her make-up from the show.

Friday's edition of the ITV show began at 10:00 BST with Hammond and her regular co-host O'Leary at the helm, before she left at 11:30 during a segment about pets.

O'Leary, 53, addressed her absence when the show returned from a break, saying: "Welcome back to This Morning, Alison is feeling a little unwell, so she's just had to duck out. Hopefully she'll be back."

He later updated viewers that she would, in fact, not be returning, "so I'll be here for the rest of the show".

Hammond initially rose to fame as contestant on Channel 4 reality show Big Brother before appearing on I'm A Celebrity and Strictly Come Dancing.

She became a co-host in This Morning in 2021, and was part of the team that won a National Television Award for best daytime programme the following year.

She joined Bake Off in 2023 and took over from the late Paul O'Grady on For the Love of Dogs in 2024.

articles.title: ‘That’s 100% him’: Newly released video shows moment police arrest Luigi Mangione
articles.summary: Newly released body camera footage shows the moment Pennsylvania police confront Luigi Mangione in a McDonald’s and later find a gun, a magazine and a silencer in his backpack.
articles.body: Newly released body camera footage shows the moment Pennsylvania police confront Luigi Mangione in a McDonald’s and later find a gun, a magazine and a silencer in his backpack. In the footage, officers approach Mangione and ask him to pull down his face mask. “Yeah, sure,” Mangione says. An officer appears to immediately recognize him as the suspect in the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson. “That’s 100% him,” an officer says, standing outside the Altoona McDonald’s. “I told you, man,” another says. CNN first reported on the videos and said they were shown during a suppression hearing last year but were not made public until now. NBC News has obtained copies. Thompson, 50, was shot in the back on Dec. 4, 2024, as he headed to a UnitedHealthcare investor conference in Manhattan. Security video shows Mangione approaching him from behind and opening fire. Thompson was pronounced dead at a hospital. Mangione was arrested at the McDonald’s five days later, after he was recognized from photos released by police. In the footage, officers say Mangione had checked into a hostel with fake identification and ask him about the name he used. “Is that your name, Mark Rosario?” an officer asks. “Uh, no, sir,” Mangione says, seated with his arms crossed. He then gives his real name. Officers search his backpack at the McDonald’s and find a gun magazine. “It’s f---ing him, dude,” an officer says. “It’s f---ing him. 100%.” Mangione was taken to a police station, where officers found more items, including a gun, a silencer, a gun magazine hidden in a pair of underwear and a journal with handwritten notes. “He has a handgun, suppressor, his cellphone’s in a Faraday bag. He has a checklist for today. Tomorrow he’s supposed to do an intel check-in and get a survival kit,” another officer says, speaking on the phone. In August, Mangione pleaded guilty to federal stalking charges. In a statement to the court, he said that in 2024 he posed as a potential investor managing more than $50 billion in assets and emailed UnitedHealthcare executives to confirm the location of the investors conference so he could track Thompson. Mangione, who comes from a prominent Baltimore family, said he traveled to New York “with the intent to shoot Brian Thompson.” He said he was driven to kill Thompson because of his experience with the healthcare system as a patient with a back injury. Prosecutors have said Mangione was never a customer and had no personal connection to the insurance giant. His state trial, which includes a second-degree murder charge, was set to begin in September, but a judge postponed it to give prosecutors time to respond to a double jeopardy motion from his attorneys. Mangione’s defense argues the state charges should be dismissed because he pleaded guilty to the federal charges.

articles.title: In 2024, Jeff Bezos' ex-wife MacKenzie Scott gave $30 million to a Silicon Valley housing nonprofit; a year later, it unveiled a 10-year plan to widen access to affordable homes in the Bay Area
articles.summary: In October 2024, Jeff Bezos’ ex-wife and philanthropist MacKenzie Scott, through her Yield Giving fund, donated $30 million to Housing Trust Silicon
articles.body: In October 2024, Jeff Bezos’ ex-wife and philanthropist MacKenzie Scott, through her Yield Giving fund, donated $30 million to Housing Trust Silicon Valley, providing the largest individual gift in the nonprofit’s history. The unrestricted donation was aimed at helping the organisation expand affordable housing opportunities across the 14-county Bay Area, one of the most expensive housing markets in the United States. As per Housing Trust TV, announcing the gift, Noni Ramos, chief executive of Housing Trust Silicon Valley, said the funding would enable the organisation to accelerate efforts to create more equitable and affordable communities. The nonprofit indicated that the money could be used to strengthen its loan fund, expand existing housing programmes and launch new initiatives focused on affordability and housing equity.The gift came through MacKenzie Scott's Yield Giving philanthropic fundThe gift, announced in October 2024, came through Scott's Yield Giving philanthropic fund and stood as the largest single donation from an individual in Housing Trust's history. Housing Trust CEO Noni Ramos described the unrestricted contribution as an incredible surprise the organization felt deeply honored and grateful to receive, noting that the trust placed in the organization also carries a responsibility to translate that generosity into meaningful, lasting impact for the communities it serves.Housing Trust's Board Chair, Joe Anzalone, framed the timing as especially significant, coming just as the organization was preparing to mark 25 years of funding affordable housing solutions. He pointed to the scale of Housing Trust's track record up to that point — having invested $615 million in the community, created more than 27,200 housing opportunities, and helped over 51,000 neighbors find affordable housing across the region, while helping leverage an additional $8.1 billion through its partners.Founded in 2000, Housing Trust was created through a partnership between affordable housing advocates, businesses, and public and private sector leaders and foundations, aimed at meeting the Bay Area's growing need for affordable housing solutions.A year later: the 10-year plan takes shapeNearly a year after the initial gift, Housing Trust unveiled a detailed 10-year plan in September 2025 for how it intends to convert the $30 million into durable, long-term housing solutions across the region — a plan the organization says was shaped through input from staff, board members, and community stakeholders.The roadmap centers on five major initiatives designed to direct the gift toward both expanded housing opportunity and stronger organizational capacity over the coming decade. According to the plan, the funding will help accelerate Housing Trust's core lending work, expand homeownership assistance programs, fuel new policy and innovation efforts, and strengthen the organization's overall long-term impact.Concretely, that includes growing Housing Trust's core revolving loan fund and piloting new financing tools tailored specifically for developers. Michael Quinn, who leads much of this development-facing work at Housing Trust, described the approach as centered on problem-solving rather than simply designing new products, emphasizing that the organization is listening closely to what developers actually need most and shaping financing accordingly — whether that means adjusting timing, pricing, or loan terms to help projects overcome common barriers. The plan also calls for extending Housing Trust's first-time homebuyer programs into a wider geographic footprint across the region in the year ahead.Real projects already benefitingEven before the 10-year plan was formalized, Housing Trust's broader work continued delivering tangible results across the Bay Area. In Sunnyvale, the organization provided a $2 million predevelopment loan in partnership with Related California to support Meridian Apartments, which created 90 affordable homes for families in one of the region's most expensive cities. In San Rafael, Housing Trust backed Eden Housing with a $4 million loan for Vivalon, a 66-unit affordable housing development for older adults that pairs affordable housing with supportive services.By the time of its 2025 Annual Report, marking its 25th anniversary, Housing Trust reported having invested more than $690 million total since its founding, helping create over 28,700 homes and open doors for roughly 53,800 neighbors across the greater Bay Area — figures that continue climbing as the MacKenzie Scott-funded plan moves into its early implementation phase.Part of a broader pattern of givingHousing Trust's gift wasn't an isolated act of generosity. MacKenzie Scott gave away roughly $2 billion in 2024 alone, spread across nearly 200 organizations focused largely on economic security, housing affordability, job stability, child development, and healthcare, bringing her five-year philanthropic total to more than $19 billion. articles.title: Poor communication marred emergency response to deadly L.A. area fires, report finds
articles.summary: A new report on the deadly 2025 fires in the Los Angeles area describes an emergency response marred by poor preparation, communication issues and leadership that struggled to coordinate between jurisdictions.
articles.body: During last year’s fires in the Los Angeles area, police dispatchers had to temporarily route 911 calls through a single captain’s personal cellphone. So many calls came in that some firefighter units went “dark” — meaning dispatchers were no longer tracking them. As communications broke down, some firefighters began to take their cues from captains they trusted instead of the agency’s top leaders. These are just a few examples of emergency communications failures described in a new, comprehensive review of the deadly fires. The findings paint a picture of a response marred by poor preparation, communication issues and disorganized leadership that struggled to coordinate between jurisdictions. The 724-page report, released Friday, comes from UL Research Institutes (ULRI), an organization that focuses on safety science. Gov. Gavin Newsom tasked the researchers with evaluating the conditions, decisions, actions and systems that influenced the conflagration. This is the second of two ULRI reports evaluating the fires. Overall, the researchers found that Los Angeles authorities were not prepared or trained for such extreme conditions and that they struggled to work side by side as the situation deteriorated. On the night the Eaton Fire took off, for example, “the speed and scale of the event overwhelmed the 911 system,” Derek Alconis, a senior research program manager and lead investigator at ULRI, said in a news briefing. “Calls came in faster than dispatch could manage or assign them.” As the situation worsened, agencies struggled to communicate, and those in charge lost track of where crews were working and what they were doing. “It was not an effective unified command,” Alconis said, adding that the confusion hampered evacuation efforts. The report confirmed previous assessments of how the Palisades Fire started: LAFD did not fully mop up an earlier burn in the area. The department did not have standards for that kind of work, the report says. The original burn, called the Lachman Fire, was the result of an alleged arson. The trial of the man accused of starting that fire ended in a mistrial this summer after the jury deadlocked. A second trial is scheduled for this fall. In a statement, LAFD said it was carefully reviewing the analysis. “While FSRI found that no single decision explains last January’s tragedy, that does not lessen LAFD’s responsibility for the decisions that were ours,” LAFD said. “The report identifies a number of areas where the LAFD must do better. They include how we confirm a fire is truly out before dangerous weather returns, how we track and direct every unit on a major fire, and how we plan and carry out evacuations with our partners. We accept those findings.” The department said it had implemented a series of changes after its own review, including improving staffing procedures during dangerous fire weather and developing protocols to ensure fires are fully extinguished. “This report holds the LAFD to a high standard, as it should,” the statement said. “We will carefully evaluate every recommendation that applies to us, continue to track our progress, and strengthen our ability to protect the communities we serve.” The Los Angeles County Sheriff’s office said it had not had time to review the report but that it is updating its 38-year-old dispatch system and bringing on 80 new dispatchers. Since the fires, it has also equipped patrol vehicles with warning sirens for evacuations and strengthened its evacuation policy and training, the office said, along with upgrading emergency communications and fire protection equipment, among other measures. The Los Angeles Police Department did not respond to a request for comment. A spokesperson for the Los Angeles County Fire Department said the agency could not comment because of pending litigation. The fires, which started during a windstorm in January 2025, killed 31 people in the Pacific Palisades and Altadena communities. The blazes destroyed more than 16,250 homes and commercial buildings. Many residents still have not returned home and have struggled to clean up contamination left by smoke and debris. Frustration over the fire response and the rebuilding effort has become a heated election issue in the Los Angeles mayoral race. The new report says, however, that the shortcomings it outlines did not drive the tragedy. Emergency responders were up against extreme fire behavior in windy conditions that made the homes themselves the fire’s fuel. “The conditions in January 2025 were perfect for fire,” said Steve Kerber, a vice president at ULRI who leads its Fire Safety Research Institute. “The speed, scale and complexity of the Palisades and Eaton fires exceeded many of the capabilities of the systems designed to support suppression.” Many of the 175 findings in the report will not come as a surprise to those who have followed the flurry of lawsuits, investigative news reports and city and county after-action reviews. But it offers a comprehensive picture of what went wrong, as well as something of a road map for the wind-driven urban firestorms that are growing more common across the West. Among its 266 recommendations are to increase training opportunities for wildfire and incident management in California, to equip command staff with portable satellite internet kits in case of communication failures, and to train firefighters to use water from residential pools. The report describes plenty of successes, as well. The authors said that the National Weather Service effectively communicated the extreme fire weather threat, and it credited a program of volunteers called Community Brigade with helping residents to evacuate. Private fire companies, too, helped save some structures and prevent fire spread, it says, though the report acknowledges that private firefighting is controversial. ULRI also produced an after-action report about the 2023 Lahaina fires in Maui, an effort the authors said they were just finishing when the Palisades and Eaton fires took off. They immediately saw similarities between the events, in which fast-spreading, wind-driven fires overwhelmed fire departments. To understand what went wrong in Los Angeles, the researchers behind the report evaluated in person more than 900 structures that burned and interviewed 200 residents and 295 people working at 22 agencies involved in the fire response. The team reviewed 911 calls, radio communications, dispatch data, evacuation maps, staffing plans and more. However, many agencies, including LAFD and LAPD, did not provide records the report authors requested more than a year ago, they said, leaving key gaps in the assessment. For example, the authors said they did not get copies of emergency evacuation plans or records about the response to the Lachman Fire. And LAPD did not provide dispatch or radio communications or reports from officers and supervisors, they said. Kerber said the L.A. area blazes demonstrated how fire safety no longer depends on the actions of a single homeowner or government agency. “Risk increasingly operates at the neighborhood and regional level … future resilience depends on coordinated action across the entire system rather than on improvements made by one property owner or agency at a time,” he said.

articles.title: Russian aerial strikes snarl traffic on 3 Kyiv bridges in a new disruption tactic
articles.summary: KYIV, Ukraine — Russian aerial attacks forced the partial closure Friday of three bridges over the Dnipro River in Kyiv, the Ukrainian capital’s mayor said, in Moscow’s latest effort to disrupt life in the city.
articles.body: KYIV, Ukraine — Russian aerial attacks forced the partial closure Friday of three bridges over the Dnipro River in Kyiv, the Ukrainian capital’s mayor said, in Moscow’s latest effort to disrupt life in the city. Meanwhile, Ukraine’s top diplomat said officials have received separate proposals for a partial truce with Russia from the United States, India, Turkey and Egypt. The proposals envision halting attacks on energy infrastructure, which have caused fuel shortages in Russia and power outages in Ukraine, and on Black Sea shipping needed to get vital grain exports to world markets. The Russian strikes forcing the full or partial closure of three of Kyiv’s six road bridges caused traffic logjams and appeared to be a new tactic in its campaign to torment the city’s residents. Previously, Russia has hit apartment blocks, supermarket warehouses, gas stations and data centers, among other targets, in an escalation of attacks. Oleksandr Pihalo, a Kyiv resident, said traffic was “jammed solid” and it took him 45 minutes to cover 4 kilometers (2 ½ miles). “It’s a total mess on the road today,” he told The Associated Press. One of the three bridges was hit again on Friday afternoon, Mayor Vitalii Klitschko said. Civilians “are bearing the brunt of this war,” the U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Türk, said in Geneva on Friday. “The war in Ukraine is a human rights catastrophe that is growing and intensifying by the week, causing unfathomable pain to civilians,” he said. “Across Ukraine, people are living in constant dread.” While the aerial war has intensified in recent months, fighting along the roughly 1,250-kilometer front line snaking through northern, eastern and southern Ukraine has been virtually deadlocked. Russia invaded its neighbor more than 4 ½ years ago, and there are no concrete signs that a peace settlement might be possible. However, Ukraine has this year made some progress against Russia’s bigger army, according to the Institute for the Study of War. Russian forces lost control over almost 300 square kilometers (116 square miles) of Ukraine between March and September, the Washington-based think tank said in a report late Thursday. Also, it said that the Russian military suffered over 46,000 casualties in September, the highest monthly number this year. It did not say how many Ukrainian troops were killed or wounded. Zelenskyy says sanctions can stop Russian drones and missiles Russia fired more than 100 drones at Ukraine overnight, striking Kyiv and eight other regions, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. Almost half of the drones were the jet-powered type that are especially hard to stop, he said. A drone hit a high-rise apartment block in Kyiv, killing one person, he said. At least four people were reported wounded elsewhere. Zelenskyy repeated his appeal for foreign countries to close loopholes in international sanctions on Russia and to add more restrictions on its trade. He said Russia’s drones and missiles are “critically dependent” on foreign components. “Every Russian drone can actually be stopped right at the production line,” Zelenskyy said in a post on X. Ukraine has also bombarded Russia with the long-range drones and missiles it now produces, aiming at military manufacturing plants and oil refineries. The Russian Defense Ministry said Friday that its air defenses overnight downed 646 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions, occupied Crimea, the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea. One person was wounded in Russia’s southwestern Volgograd region, Gov. Andrei Bocharov said. The attack targeted “industrial infrastructure,” he said, without providing details. Ukraine is ready for a truce on energy strikes and the Black Sea Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the partial truce proposals presented to Kyiv by four countries were the first time India has offered to play a role. India is trying to balance its ties with Russia against its growing partnerships with the United States and other Western powers. A new U.S. sanctions package on Russia could impose up to 100% tariffs on New Delhi as a major importer of Russian oil. Sybiha said Kyiv is ready to accept a ceasefire if it stops Russian attacks on Ukraine’s power grid — as well as Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries — and on cargo vessels exporting grain and other farm products through the Black Sea. “We are ready for an energy and Black Sea ceasefire, but only in that combination. Energy and a ceasefire in the Black Sea,” Sybiha told reporters Thursday, in comments embargoed until Friday. He repeated Ukraine’s offer of an unconditional ceasefire on the front line. But Moscow has rejected a ceasefire, saying a comprehensive peace deal must be agreed rather than a temporary truce. Russia’s Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said Friday that Ukraine attacked four Russian oil refineries overnight, but air defenses fended off the attacks and key equipment wasn’t damaged. The government and companies have worked hard to improve protection of refineries, he said. Russian President Vladimir Putin decreed in August that the state can temporarily seize control of critical infrastructure facilities if private owners fail to protect them or rebuild them after Ukrainian strikes. It wasn’t possible to verify either side’s claims. Sybiha said Ukraine is requesting some 300 Patriot missiles from partner countries because intelligence services estimate that Russia is holding 600 ballistic missiles in reserve and can produce up to 140 ballistic missiles per month. The U.S.-made Patriot air defense systems can effectively defend against ballistic missiles, which fly fast and drop steeply, but they are in short supply due to the Iran war. Ukraine needs more funding and quickly, foreign minister says Ukraine urgently needs funding in order to contract future drone production, so there are no gaps in supply at the beginning of next year, Sybiha said. Kyiv faces a projected budget deficit of roughly $27 billion this year, although the European Union has promised to help meet its financial requirements. The European Commission announced Friday it had disbursed $3.3 billion to Ukraine in its latest batch of financing. Zelenskyy said the amount would help Ukraine’s financial stability and strengthen its defense. Russia is also facing economic and financial challenges due to high military spending and debt.

articles.body:
Anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas has appeared in court charged with entering a restricted zone at a migrant processing centre in Dover.

The 37-year-old, also known as Danny Tommo, is accused of committing the offence on 31 March, according to court documents.

Thomas is further accused of using threatening words or behaviour in the Kent town on 1 April and obstructing a person engaged in a lawful activity on 6 April.

He is also charged with entering or remaining in Dover Docks without having lawful business or permission, the documents say.

Thomas faces another charge of racially aggravated harassment by allegedly using threatening or abusive words.

He appeared at Margate Magistrates' Court on Friday via videolink wearing a grey T-shirt and rosary beads.

District Judge William Nelson sent his case for a further case management hearing at Westminster Magistrates' Court on 4 November.

Earlier this week, Thomas was refused bail during a crown court hearing over the alleged slashing of a dinghy in the English Channel.

articles.title: Fires, clashes and mass arrests as student protests turn violent in France: Video
articles.summary: France’s student protests turned violent on Friday, with fires burning across cities, clashes between protesters and riot police and hundreds of schools
articles.body: France’s student protests turned violent on Friday, with fires burning across cities, clashes between protesters and riot police and hundreds of schools disrupted as a movement over education conditions spread nationwide. The ministry of national education said 564 schools were affected on Friday, while nearly 400 high schools were expected to remain closed.Images from Paris and surrounding areas showed burning barricades and rubbish bins, while protesters confronted police in several cities. Riot police used tear gas and made arrests as authorities moved to clear blockades outside schools.The protests began last week in the Paris region over overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages and deteriorating school buildings before spreading across the country. More than 1,200 high schools have been disrupted or blocked at some point during the mobilisation, education minister Edouard Geffray said, according to BFMTV.Geffray said the movement had “changed in nature” and was “being hijacked by violent groups”. He also said nearly 400 high schools were expected to be closed on Friday.The unrest intensified on Thursday, when authorities reported fires at schools and attacks on staff. In Marseille, police said protesters surrounded a fire truck responding to a blaze at Saint-Exupery high school, forced firefighters to leave and then set the vehicle alight. A headteacher at Victor Hugo high school was also attacked and injured, prosecutors said.Police reported more than 1,900 arrests on Thursday, while 305 officers were injured, according to the interior ministry. Authorities have also reported injuries among students and school staff.The government has said it respects the right to peaceful protest but has ordered police to break up blockades and respond to violence and vandalism. Officials said fireworks and other projectiles had been used against police and school staff, while the interior ministry alleged that people intent on destruction had joined the student movement.Students, meanwhile, say they are protesting conditions they consider inadequate, including long school days, staff shortages and overcrowded classrooms. The demonstrations have also drawn university students and spread beyond France, with protests reported in Belgium.The unrest comes as France heads towards its next presidential election, adding a political dimension to the protests.You use AI every day. articles.title: ‘I want the truth’: NY governor appoints prosecutor in Cornell rape case
articles.summary: New York Governor Kathy Hochul says local authorities failed to properly investigate the 2024 allegations.
articles.body:
New York Governor Kathy Hochul has appointed state Attorney General Letitia James as a special prosecutor to investigate an alleged gang rape at Cornell University, saying newly released information had undermined her confidence in the local prosecutor’s handling of the case.

In a news conference on Friday, Hochul said that the woman who reported the alleged assault had been failed by institutions responsible for protecting her, including Cornell University Police and the Tompkins County district attorney’s office.

“In what world does the district attorney not even interview her, or anyone else involved, or even request the full transcript?” Hochul asked at the news conference. “And I want the truth. I think every parent in this state, every New Yorker wants the truth in this case.”

Hochul signed an executive order on Thursday requiring the attorney general to investigate the alleged October 2024 assault. If warranted, evidence will be presented to a grand jury and the case prosecuted.

The order states the Tompkins County district attorney declined to prosecute the case in November 2024 without speaking to Jane Doe and relied, at least in part, on information from a Cornell police statement that omitted her assertion that she had been sexually assaulted.

The appointment of James means the state attorney general’s office, rather than the county district attorney, will now control the criminal investigation.

Prosecutors initially closed the case without criminal charges in 2024. Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten reopened the investigation on Monday, after Jane Doe filed a civil lawsuit accusing seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity of sexually assaulting her.

Van Houten has defended his original decision, saying in a September 28 statement that prosecutors reviewed a six-page sworn statement the woman gave Cornell police in November 2024.

He said the statement did not allege that she had been drugged against her will, and described her participation in sexual conduct as voluntary and consensual. He said multiple prosecutors and investigators reviewed the statement and concluded that, as presented, the facts did not establish a crime under New York law.

The governor, however, said the full account given to police was not conveyed to prosecutors. She cited reports that Jane Doe told investigators she was “100% confident” she had been raped.

Cornell has said its police department provided prosecutors with the evidence it had gathered, including a Snapchat screenshot, and that the university separately investigated the allegations through its disciplinary process. Cornell said sanctions imposed after that process included expulsions and suspensions.

Cornell has also said it is conducting an independent review of how it handled the allegations.

The Cornell case has renewed debate over New York’s definition of incapacity to consent. Under current state law, a person is considered “mentally incapacitated” when drugs or alcohol are given to someone without consent.

A state bill introduced in June would extend the provision to cases in which a victim voluntarily consumed alcohol or drugs but became so intoxicated that they were temporarily unable to control their conduct, if the accused knew or reasonably should have known of the victim’s condition.

The legislation has gained renewed attention following the Cornell allegations. Lawmakers said on Thursday that the case highlighted what they described as a gap in the state’s current law.

“If someone is too intoxicated to consent, it should not matter whether they chose to use drugs or alcohol,” Hochul said at Friday’s news conference. “Voluntary intoxication is not a licence for sexual assault or gang rape, period.”

Lindsey Boylan, a New York City Council candidate and the first woman to accuse former Governor Andrew Cuomo of sexual harassment publicly, said Hochul should use the moment to push for broader legislative change.

“I expect to see her follow through with not just supporting the independent investigation, but also changing the state laws,” Boylan said. “That is what I’m expecting her to do now, and I think that is what every survivor is expecting her to do now.”

articles.title: A Maryland homeowner received an unsolicited $234,368.25 check tied to an offer for her property; a state law that took effect on October 1 now bans sending such checks with unsolicited purchase offers
articles.summary: A homeowner in Parkville, a suburb of Baltimore, opened her mail one day to find an unexpected check for $234,368.25 (£176,000) made out to her.
articles.body: A homeowner in Parkville, a suburb of Baltimore, opened her mail one day to find an unexpected check for $234,368.25 (£176,000) made out to her. It was not a lottery prize or a bank mistake. Instead, it was a tactic used by a potential buyer who wanted to purchase her home without putting it on the open market. That practice is now banned across Maryland under a state law that took effect on 1 October. The law targets an aggressive type of direct-mail marketing. It makes it illegal to send property owners negotiable financial instruments along with unsolicited offers to buy their homes. The legislation, called Senate Bill 582, was signed into law by Maryland Governor Wes Moore in April. Anyone who violates the ban can face a misdemeanor charge and a fine of up to $500 (£375).Deceptive tactics targeting vulnerable ownersDirect-mail offers from real estate investors are common across North America. Homeowners often receive postcards, letters, and phone calls offering quick, all-cash deals without real estate agent fees or the need to make home repairs. However, consumer groups told Maryland lawmakers that sending an actual check can make the offer seem much more real to a homeowner. During legislative hearings, Jennifer Bevan-Dangel, president and chief executive of the advocacy group Economic Action Maryland, described the checks as risky tools. She said that even experienced advisers were surprised by them and were unsure about the real legal meaning of these unsolicited messages. She called the approach deceptive at worst and misleading at best. Representatives of the CASH Campaign of Maryland, a nonprofit group focused on financial security for low-income residents, also testified that these checks can look like an easy source of money for people facing financial trouble. The group warned that cashing or depositing the checks could quietly bind people to contracts they do not fully understand.Historical roots in consumer lendingThe strategy is based on live check financing, a direct-mail lending method that became widely used during the 1990s. Banks and other financial companies mailed active loan checks to consumers who had not applied for them. By depositing the money, recipients agreed to the loan terms, including interest rates and service fees. A 1998 investigation by the US Government Accountability Office showed how large the practice had become. The report said Fleet Bank mailed 50,000 live checks during a limited trial in 1995. By March 1998, the bank had sent 5.85 million checks, resulting in about 155,000 individual loans worth $680 million (£510 million). The fast growth of the practice also created major security risks. Fleet Bank recorded 68 confirmed cases of fraud involving intercepted checks. Another lender, First Chicago, stopped its live check program completely after suffering financial losses it could not sustain. States began placing limits on the practice around the same time. Minnesota introduced rules in 1998 that restricted live check mailings unless the recipient had specifically asked for them. North Carolina required clear disclosures in 2001. Despite those measures, the practice later returned. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau responded by issuing updated guidance after direct-mail loan offers increased.Legal safeguards and official guidanceUnder the updated Maryland law, a homeowner does not automatically enter into a legal agreement just because an unsolicited check arrives in the mail. Legal responsibility applies only if the recipient signs and negotiates the financial instrument. State regulators are telling residents who receive unexpected financial offers by mail not to sign, endorse, or deposit them. The Maryland Office of Financial Regulation is asking residents to report suspicious documents directly to officials so they can be investigated. The law also contains specific exceptions. Financial institutions can still send convenience checks connected to existing lines of credit. Prescreened offers for unsecured credit that are regulated under federal law are also not covered by the ban.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
